faq.a: Holding breath stops chest wall movement, eliminating the friction between inflamed pericardial layers.
faq.q: Why does the rub disappear when the patient holds their breath?

faq.a: It is uncommon; chronic inflammation usually leads to thickening or constriction rather than a rub.
faq.q: Can a pericardial rub be heard in chronic pericarditis?

faq.a: Colchicine is generally avoided in pregnancy due to limited safety data; use NSAIDs with caution.

exam: A 28‑year‑old HIV‑positive man presents with pleuritic chest pain relieved by sitting up. What bedside maneuver will most likely reveal a pericardial rub? — Ask the patient to lean forward and listen at the left lower sternal border with the diaphragm; a triphasic scratchy sound confirms the rub.

You hear a pericardial rub but the ECG is normal. How do you proceed? — Recognise early pericarditis can have a normal ECG; obtain an echocardiogram to assess for effusion and start empirical NSAIDs while arranging further work‑up.

A patient with TB pericarditis has a large effusion but is haemodynamically stable. What is the next best step? — Initiate anti‑TB therapy and give adjunctive steroids; monitor for tamponade and arrange pericardiocentesis only if signs of compromise develop.

What feature distinguishes a pericardial friction rub from a pleural friction rub? — The pericardial rub is heard best at the left lower sternal border and persists throughout the cardiac cycle, whereas a pleural rub is localized to lung fields and varies with respiration.

During assessment you note hypotension, muffled heart sounds, and JVD. How does this change your management? — These are Beck’s triad for tamponade; perform urgent pericardiocentesis or arrange immediate transfer for drainage.

Why is colchicine added to NSAIDs in acute pericarditis? — Colchicine reduces recurrence rates by inhibiting neutrophil chemotaxis; it is especially useful in viral or idiopathic cases where steroids are not indicated.

A patient on high‑dose ibuprofen develops renal impairment. What alternative anti‑inflammatory can you use? — Switch to aspirin (if not contraindicated) or consider low‑dose corticosteroids, weighing infection risk.

How would you differentiate constrictive pericarditis from restrictive cardiomyopathy on exam? — Constrictive pericarditis shows a pericardial knock and prominent Kussmaul’s sign; restrictive cardiomyopathy lacks a pericardial rub and has a more uniform diastolic dysfunction.
ai.title: Pericardial Friction Rub
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: A pericardial friction rub is a scratchy, triphasic sound heard over the heart when inflamed pericardium rubs against the chest wall. It is a key bedside clue to acute pericarditis, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: Triphasic sound: systolic, early diastolic, late diastolic components
Increases when patient sits up and leans forward
sections.p: Acute pericarditis is inflammation of the pericardial sac. The most characteristic sign is a pericardial friction rub, best heard with the diaphragm of the stethoscope at the left lower sternal border, patient leaning forward.

b: Chest pain: sharp, pleuritic, improves when sitting up
ECG: diffuse ST‑segment elevation and PR depression
sections.p: Diagnostic criteria for acute pericarditis require at least two of: chest pain characteristic of pericarditis, pericardial rub, ECG changes, new or worsening pericardial effusion.

b: TB pericarditis often presents with a dry rub and a large effusion
HIV patients may have atypical presentations and co‑infection
sections.p: In East African hospitals, common causes include viral infections (e.g., Coxsackie), tuberculosis, HIV‑related opportunistic infections, rheumatic fever, and post‑myocardial infarction (Dressler) syndrome.

t.b: Does the patient have diffuse ST elevation/PR depression? Confirms pericardial inflammation.
Is there an enlarged cardiac silhouette suggesting effusion? Helps stage severity.
Is there pericardial fluid or tamponade? Guides urgent management; if unavailable, rely on clinical tamponade signs.
What is the cause? Look for TB PCR, acid‑fast bacilli, lymphocyte predominance.
Is immunosuppression contributing? Influences antimicrobial choice.

b: NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen) as first‑line anti‑inflammatory unless contraindicated
Colchicine added to reduce recurrence, especially in viral or idiopathic cases
For TB pericarditis: standard anti‑TB regimen (rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) plus steroids if large effusion
In HIV: optimise antiretroviral therapy and treat opportunistic pathogens
If tamponade suspected: urgent pericardiocentesis; if not possible, arrange transfer
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, relieve inflammation, and monitor for complications such as tamponade or constriction.

b: Pleural friction rub: heard over the lung fields, disappears with breath holding
Murmurs: continuous, vary with cardiac cycle, not scratchy
Bronchial breath sounds: harsh, not triphasic
sections.p: Other thoracic sounds can mimic a rub.

b: Early TB pericarditis may have a bland fluid analysis
Steroid use can mask fever and pain, delaying diagnosis
sections.p: Normal ECG does not exclude pericarditis early; a small effusion may be missed on plain X‑ray.

b: Ask for the effect of posture on the rub
Link diffuse ST changes to pericardial inflammation
Differentiate tamponade (Beck’s triad) from uncomplicated pericarditis
sections.p: Exam questions often test integration of history, exam, and investigations.

whenToSeekHelp: Signs of cardiac tamponade: hypotension, muffled heart sounds, jugular venous distension
Persistent high fever or sepsis in an immunocompromised patient
